Need to search first.I've put together notes on Revelation 18, but the research is incomplete. The search tool hit its usage limit partway through, and I couldn't open any full page; everything below comes from the excerpts that searches returned. Wesley's notes on chapter 18 were the one source that came through in full. **I found nothing from Lutheran sources, Orthodox sources, bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org notes, or prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teachers on this chapter**, so those parts are missing.

## The main disagreement: who is "Babylon"?
Most of the disagreement in the sources flows from this one question.
- **Papal Rome (the historicist view: the chapter as church history):**
  - Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/revelation-18.html
  - Barnes: the papacy, not the city itself. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/revelation-18.html
  - Wesley: https://www.ccel.org/w/wesley/notes/notes/Revelation.html
  - Ironside: Rome, but also a worldwide system of apostasy; he rejects the idea of a rebuilt Babylon. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/revelation-18.html
- **Pagan Rome of John's day (the first-century view):**
  - Ligonier (Reformed): https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/coming-out-of-babylon
  - Barclay: he calls the chapter a "doom song" over Rome. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/revelation-18.html
- **The end-times world system under Antichrist (the futurist view):**
  - Guzik (enduringword): the Babylon of ch. 17 is religious and is judged mid-Tribulation; the Babylon of ch. 18 is commercial and is judged at the end. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-18/
  - MacArthur: holds the same two-Babylon view. https://gty.org/library/sermons-library/66-63/babylon-is-fallen-part-1
  - Precept Austin: insists chs. 17 and 18 describe one Babylon, a literal city that will be rebuilt. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-18-commentary
  - bible.org: a rebuilt city on the Euphrates. https://bible.org/seriespage/25-destruction-commercial-babylon-rev-181-24
  - Chuck Smith: the city may be rebuilt as Antichrist's capital. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/csc/revelation-18.html
- **A symbol of the satanic world system:** Constable quotes Johnson for this view. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/revelation-18.html
- **Got Questions** surveys all of these views. https://www.gotquestions.org/Babylon-the-Great-has-fallen.html
- **Catholic view:** Babylon is pagan Rome or apostate Jerusalem, and it cannot be the Catholic Church.
  - https://www.catholic.com/tract/the-whore-of-babylon
  - https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/hunt-ing-the-whore-of-babylon-part-ii

## Verse-by-verse notes

**v. 1**
- Wesley says the angel is called "another" in contrast with the angel of 10:1. If a servant shines this brightly, imagine the Lord. https://www.ccel.org/w/wesley/notes/notes/Revelation.html
- Guzik: the angel is so recently from God's presence that he glows. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-18/
- Gill thinks the angel is not Christ but probably a minister, or ministers, of the gospel. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/revelation-18.html
- Precept Austin sees the light as a preview of the Millennial Kingdom (Isa. 60:1–3). https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-18-commentary

**v. 2**
- "Fallen, fallen" is repeated like a funeral song. It describes complete desolation, echoing Isa. 13 and 21:9.
  - Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-18/
  - Ellicott, who sees a moral meaning too: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/18.htm
- Gill says the verse describes the city after its ruin, when people will never live there again. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/revelation-18.html
- Wesley teases Catholics: if this means heathen Rome, devils would be its only residents for ever. https://www.ccel.org/w/wesley/notes/notes/Revelation.html
- Ligonier links the verse to Rome's population collapse in later centuries. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/coming-out-of-babylon
- Precept Austin connects the fall to the seventh bowl (16:19). https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-18-commentary
- Ironside says the "demons" show the apostate church's true source. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/revelation-18.html

**v. 3**
- Ellicott: she has harmed humanity in three forms: nations, kings and merchants. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/18.htm
- Gill reads the "merchants" as dealers in pardons, indulgences and Masses for souls. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/revelation-18.html
- Matthew Henry: she drew people into spiritual adultery and held them with her wealth. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rev/Rev_018.cfm
- Precept Austin: her pollution reaches politics, trade and religion, and goes back to Babel. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-18-commentary

**v. 4 (the most debated verse)**
- All sources agree the verse echoes Isa. 48:20, Isa. 52:11 and Jer. 51:6, 45. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/18-4.html
- Whose voice is it?
  - God's, according to Barnes. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/18-4.html
  - Christ's, according to Wesley. https://www.ccel.org/w/wesley/notes/notes/Revelation.html
  - Another angel speaking for God, according to the Pulpit Commentary. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/18-4.htm
- What does "come out" mean? The traditions disagree:
  - **Leave the Roman church.**
    - Barnes says the verse "will not only justify the Reformation" but made staying in the papal church sinful once its wickedness was plain. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown agrees that God has people even in the Roman church, but they must leave at once. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/18-4.htm
    - Gill means both leaving the church's communion and literally leaving the city, as Lot left Sodom. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/revelation-18.html
  - **Not a physical exit.**
    - Ellicott: "not to be understood of a bodily exodus from Rome." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/18.htm
    - Lance Ralston (enduringword): a moral and spiritual departure. Its first application is to Tribulation believers after the Rapture, but it applies to us too. https://post.enduringword.com/come-out/
  - **Materialism.** Guzik: the commercial lure is a constant threat to believers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-18/
  - **Literal, for the future.** Precept Austin: it concerns Tribulation saints and the literal city. It warns that "legalistic shepherds" misuse the verse to control their flocks. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-18-commentary
  - **Ligonier (Reformed):** first-century believers were told to avoid Rome's trade-guild idolatry, as at Thyatira and Laodicea. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/coming-out-of-babylon
  - **Coffman:** God has a people even in the harlot church. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/18-4.html

**v. 5**
- Guzik: her sins are piled up like the tower of Babel. God remembers her sins but forgets believers' sins (Heb. 8:12). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-18/
- Wesley: "even to heaven" means the highest guilt. https://www.ccel.org/w/wesley/notes/notes/Revelation.html

**v. 6 (who is told to repay her?)**
- Wesley: God speaking to those who carry out his vengeance. https://www.ccel.org/w/wesley/notes/notes/Revelation.html
- Gill: God's people, chiefly the seven bowl angels and the ten kings. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/revelation-18.html
- Barnes: the nations she oppressed. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/revelation-18.html
- Geneva notes: the godly act like the Levites of Exod. 32:27. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/18-4.htm
- Henry: private revenge is forbidden, but God's people may act under him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rev/Rev_018.cfm
- Light of Israel takes the opposite line: Christians are never told to judge Babylon; God uses the Beast. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/18-4.html
- What does "double" mean?
  - Wesley: a Hebrew idiom for full repayment. https://www.ccel.org/w/wesley/notes/notes/Revelation.html
  - Guzik: the double repayment for theft (Exod. 22), hinting her wealth was dishonestly gained. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-18/
- Constable: the cup she used to seduce others becomes her punishment. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/revelation-18.html

**v. 7**
- Wesley links "sit as queen" to the papal "see" (seat). "No widow" is her claim to be Christ's spouse. https://www.ccel.org/w/wesley/notes/notes/Revelation.html
- Guzik names her three sins: self-indulgence, pride and avoiding suffering. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-18/
- Barclay: pride was Rome's supreme sin (Isa. 47). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/18-7.html

**v. 8**
- Wesley: famine replaces luxury, and her strength cannot stand against the "strong" Lord. https://www.ccel.org/w/wesley/notes/notes/Revelation.html
- Barnes mentions volcanic features near Rome, such as Lake Vico. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/revelation-18.html
- Henry: the suddenness makes the misery worse. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rev/Rev_018.cfm

**vv. 9–10**
- Henry: they mourn their punishment, not their sin, which is "worldly sorrow". Her friends keep their distance. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rev/Rev_018.cfm
- Guzik notes that some think nuclear weapons are meant. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-18/
- Ironside suggests the burning might be literal. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/revelation-18.html
- Wesley: Rome's ancient name meant "strong". https://www.ccel.org/w/wesley/notes/notes/Revelation.html
- Barnes: the kings could not save her. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/revelation-18.html

**vv. 11–13**
- Guzik: the cargo is luxuries, not necessities, and the merchants' grief is self-interest. "Bodies and souls of men" applies today to trafficking and pornography. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-18/
- Wesley: these goods were still used in Rome's worship. "Chariots" is a Latin word, and souls are "bought and sold at Rome". https://www.ccel.org/w/wesley/notes/notes/Revelation.html
- Gill: souls are traded through purgatory and indulgences. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/revelation-18.html
- Barclay gives historical detail on Roman luxury: silver, coverlets, marble and incense. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/revelation-18.html
- Ligonier: when Rome falls, safe travel and trade collapse. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/the-fall-of-babylon

**v. 14**
- Guzik: hell will be a place of unfulfilled desire. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-18/
- Henry: the church may fall for a time and rise again, but Babylon will not. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rev/Rev_018.cfm
- Wesley and Gill both read "fruit" as autumn fruit.
  - https://www.ccel.org/w/wesley/notes/notes/Revelation.html
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/revelation-18.html

**vv. 15–19**
- Wesley: the imagery comes from the fall of Tyre (Ezek. 26–28). https://www.ccel.org/w/wesley/notes/notes/Revelation.html
- Precept Austin: the seafarers fit Babylon better than Rome, which "had no seaport". https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-18-commentary
- Gill reads the shipmasters as religious orders. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/revelation-18.html
- MacArthur: if this city can't survive, nothing can. Dust on the head is an ancient sign of grief. https://www.gty.org/library/sermons-library/66-65/babylon-is-fallen-part-3

**v. 20**
- Wesley: all heaven rejoices, especially apostles and prophets. https://www.ccel.org/w/wesley/notes/notes/Revelation.html
- Henry: God is defending his people's cause. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rev/Rev_018.cfm
- Catholic.com: the apostles were killed, so the city must have existed in the first century. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/hunt-ing-the-whore-of-babylon-part-ii

**v. 21**
- The image comes from Jer. 51:63–64.
  - Ligonier: https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/the-fall-of-babylon
  - Wesley: https://www.ccel.org/w/wesley/notes/notes/Revelation.html
- Guzik also links it to Jesus' millstone warning. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-18/
- Coffman: "no more at all" occurs six times and is too final for pagan Rome alone. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/18-21.html
- Precept Austin: since ancient Babylon was never destroyed this way, it must be rebuilt. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-18-commentary

**v. 22**
- Wesley: rich, middle-class and poor alike will vanish. https://www.ccel.org/w/wesley/notes/notes/Revelation.html
- bible.org: industry will go silent. https://bible.org/seriespage/25-destruction-commercial-babylon-rev-181-24
- Catholic.com: these are scenes of ordinary city life, not of Vatican City. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/hunt-ing-the-whore-of-babylon-part-ii

**v. 23**
- What is the "sorcery"?
  - Guzik: the Greek word relates to drugs, so it works like addiction fed by advertising. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-18/
  - Gill: false doctrine and idolatry. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/revelation-18.html
  - bible.org: a deception by the super-rich. https://bible.org/seriespage/25-destruction-commercial-babylon-rev-181-24
- Wesley: being great merchants was neutral in itself but led to pride. https://www.ccel.org/w/wesley/notes/notes/Revelation.html

**v. 24**
- Wesley: the blood includes even deaths before the city existed (Matt. 23:35). He says no city's blood-guilt is as clear as Rome's. https://www.ccel.org/w/wesley/notes/notes/Revelation.html
- Gill: she is guilty of deaths throughout the empire. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/revelation-18.html
- Ironside: only a worldwide system fits this verse. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/revelation-18.html

If you'd like, I can try again later to fill the gaps (Lutheran, Orthodox, NET notes, Bible Odyssey, and popular modern teaching) and read the full Gill, Ellicott and Precept Austin pages.
